prompt: In an allow policy, what does one binding hold?

choices.text: One principal and every role it holds
choices.why: The policy is organised by role, not by principal.

choices.text: A role and its principals
choices.why: Right. A role appears once, with every principal that holds it.

choices.text: One permission and the resource it applies to
choices.why: Bindings name roles; permissions live inside the roles.

choices.text: A deny rule and its exceptions
choices.why: That is a deny policy, a separate kind of policy.

prompt: Why does `gcloud ... add-iam-policy-binding` start by calling `getIamPolicy`?
hint: Is there a call that adds one member?

choices.text: To check the caller is an Owner
choices.why: Permission is checked by Google on the write. The read is for the policy itself.

choices.text: Because the emulator demands it
choices.why: The CLI does the same against Google. The emulator just cannot answer the read.

choices.text: To back the policy up before changing it
choices.why: Nothing is kept. The copy it reads is the copy it edits and writes back.

choices.text: No call exists that adds one member
choices.why: Right. There is no add-one-member call; the CLI does read, modify, write in one command.

prompt: Two administrators read a project's policy at the same moment, each adds a member and writes back. What stops the second write from erasing the first one's change?
hint: A field in the policy says which version a copy was read at.

choices.text: The etag the copy was read at
choices.why: Right. The second client reads again and retries, and both members end up in the policy.

choices.text: The version field, which must be 3
choices.why: Version 3 is about conditions. It does nothing for two writers.

choices.text: Nothing; the last write wins
choices.why: That is what would happen without the etag, or with a client that drops it.

choices.text: IAM locks the policy while somebody reads it
choices.why: There is no lock. The etag detects the conflict at write time instead.

prompt: The on-call group needs Pub/Sub editor during tonight's incident, and nobody trusts themselves to remember to remove it. What does IAM offer?
hint: A binding can say when it applies.

choices.text: A deny policy that starts tomorrow
choices.why: Deny policies have no start date; a condition on the grant is the tool.

choices.text: A custom role that expires
choices.why: Roles do not expire. The binding's condition does the timing.

choices.text: A condition on `request.time`
choices.why: Right. A temporary grant ends without anybody touching it again.

choices.text: Granting Owner, which can be revoked from the console
choices.why: Owner is far more than the incident needs, and revoking it is the remembering nobody trusted.

prompt: A policy with a condition in any binding must be sent as version ___, or the conditions are dropped.
The emulator answered `getIamPolicy` with `501 UNIMPLEMENTED`. What does that mean?
hint: Lesson 1's banner said something about IAM.

choices.text: The network between the CLI and the emulator failed
choices.why: The CLI's sentence about connectivity is a guess. The emulator answered clearly.

choices.text: The topic has no policy yet
choices.why: Every topic has a policy, empty or not. The method itself is missing.

choices.text: The emulator has no IAM methods
choices.why: Right. IAM integration is disabled in the emulator, and it says so in its own way.

choices.text: The placeholder token lacks the role to read policies
choices.why: The emulator ignores the token; a permission refusal would be 403.

prompt: A `google_project_iam_binding` for `roles/viewer` lists two groups. Last month somebody granted Viewer to Ana by hand. What does the next apply do to Ana?
hint: The binding owns the whole role.

choices.text: Removes her from Viewer
choices.why: Right. `_binding` is authoritative for the role: its members are exactly the file's.

choices.text: Leaves her, since she was added outside Terraform
choices.why: That is how `_member` behaves. `_binding` sets the list exactly.

choices.text: Adds her to the file
choices.why: Terraform never writes your files.

choices.text: Fails, because the policy changed outside Terraform
choices.why: It succeeds, and that is the problem: it quietly removes her.

prompt: Why does Google's provider documentation warn against `google_project_iam_policy` in capital letters?
hint: It owns more than one role.

choices.text: It is slower than the other two
choices.why: Speed is not the danger. Removing every binding the file forgot is.

choices.text: It cannot carry conditions
choices.why: It can. The warning is about what it removes.

choices.text: It is deprecated and will be removed
choices.why: It is supported. It is simply the most dangerous of the three.

choices.text: It owns the owners, so a file that omits them removes them
choices.why: Right. With the owners gone, so are the people who could put them back.

prompt: A project's Terraform has both a `google_project_iam_binding` and a `google_project_iam_member` for Viewer. What happens over successive applies?
hint: One adds, the other sets exactly.

choices.text: The member is merged into the binding
choices.why: Terraform merges nothing across resources. Each one enforces its own idea.

choices.text: They fight, and the plan never settles
choices.why: Right. The member adds a principal the binding removes, on every run.

choices.text: Terraform refuses the configuration at validate
choices.why: Validation sees two valid resources; the conflict only shows at apply.

choices.text: The binding wins once and the conflict ends
choices.why: The member puts its principal back on the next apply, so it never ends.

prompt: Match each Terraform resource to what it owns.
hint: From the whole policy down to one grant.

pairs.right: one role and its member list

prompt: Owner on production should be exactly the two members of the break-glass group, and anything added by hand should disappear. Which resource fits?

choices.text: `google_project_iam_binding`
choices.why: Right. It sets the role's members exactly, and removes what was added by hand on the next apply.

choices.text: `google_project_iam_member`
choices.why: Additive: it would leave the hand-made grants in place.

choices.text: `google_project_iam_policy`
choices.why: That owns every role, not just Owner, and is the one to avoid.

choices.text: `google_iam_deny_policy`
choices.why: A deny refuses permissions; it does not decide who holds Owner.

prompt: The organisation grants Viewer to a group. Can a project's allow policy take that grant away from its projects?
hint: What can an allow policy contain?

choices.text: Yes, by leaving the group out of its own policy
choices.why: Leaving it out changes nothing; the inherited grant still applies.

choices.text: Yes, with a binding whose members are empty
choices.why: An empty binding grants nothing and removes nothing inherited.

choices.text: No: allow policies only add
choices.why: Right. Taking a grant away lower down is what a deny policy is for.

choices.text: Yes, with an organisation policy on the project
choices.why: Organisation policies constrain what may be done, not who holds a role.

prompt: Put the steps of evaluating a request in Google's order.
items: read the deny policies, organisation to resource
read the allow policies, organisation to resource
refuse if nothing granted the permission
trap: Reading the allow policies first is the slip: a deny would then be overridden by any grant, which is exactly what it exists to prevent.

prompt: In a deny rule, how is the permission to delete a topic written?
hint: With the service's address in front.

choices.text: `pubsub.topics.delete`
choices.why: That is the form roles use. A deny rule wants the service's address too.

choices.text: `pubsub.googleapis.com/topics.delete`
choices.why: Right. Deny policies write permissions with the service's domain first.

choices.text: `roles/pubsub.editor`
choices.why: A deny names permissions, not roles.

choices.text: `//pubsub.googleapis.com/topics/delete`
choices.why: That is shaped like a full resource name, not a permission.

prompt: The deny policy refuses project deletion to `principalSet://goog/public:all`, with the break-glass group as an exception. An Owner who is not in that group tries to delete `planner-prod`. What happens, and why?
hint: Which is read first, and does Owner matter to it?

choices.text: Allowed: Owner outranks a deny policy
choices.why: No role outranks a deny. That is the point of having one.

choices.text: Allowed: a deny on a project cannot stop its own deletion
choices.why: It can; `projects.delete` is in the list of permissions a deny supports.

choices.text: Refused: Owners may not delete projects
choices.why: Owner holds `projects.delete`. Here the deny is what refuses.

choices.text: Refused, as the deny is read first
choices.why: Right. The Owner is in `public:all` and not in the exception, so the deny refuses before any allow is read.

prompt: `deny.tf` together with `iam.tf` makes the plan add how many resources?
hint: Two from the first file, one from the second.

prompt: An auditor finds Ana holds Editor on `planner-prod` through a grant on the organisation from two years ago. The team wants her to keep Viewer there and lose every write. What is the right fix?

choices.text: Leave out Editor in `planner-prod`'s own policy
choices.why: It was never in that policy. The organisation's grant still reaches the project.

choices.text: Grant her Viewer on `planner-prod`, which replaces Editor
choices.why: Grants add up. She would hold both.

choices.text: Deny every permission to her on the organisation
choices.why: That would take away the Viewer the team wants her to keep, everywhere.

choices.text: Fix it on the organisation, where it was made
choices.why: Right. An inherited grant is fixed where it was made; nothing lower down can subtract it.
